title: The Pattern of Christ and the Path of Virtue
english: To stand even in the present and to be extended into the coming age, in which age His horn shall be lifted up in glory; that is, the kingdom which he shall be honored to attain from the saving promises. For it is customary in Scripture to call the kingdom 'Horn' (Ps 113:16).

But it is also just to establish those who worship most beautifully and consider the incorporeal as divine into something like themselves. And this would not appear to them as a curse justly, but rather becoming God is worthy of a prayer, just as they think they possess that which they marvel at.
For man is empty and a vapor in his being and non-being, because he seems to be, yet is not, but rather turns toward an image of life rather than in truth (Ps 115:2).

It is necessary for a release from the bonds of Hades, so that the God of the living and not a God of the dead may be ours, and we may be His ministers in the heavenly church, into which we return, fleeing the bonds of death (Ps 115:7-10).

He indeed rejoices as one having heard, and hopes as one receiving help; and he is strengthened by hope toward not fearing the plots of men nor marveling at their powers, but foreseeing their fall. These things indeed were formerly concerning Israel, with the other nations lying upon it (and the word is spoken hyperbolically), but after these things concerning the church from the nations, being fought against by the rebellions of the unbelievers. For those having believed in each nation were enduring the disturbances and dangers from the unbelievers, but nonetheless, even these, having been emboldened by God, conquered their opponents (Ps 117:7-9).

Those fighting serve God, yet they exult in human power and in human leadership; but those taking hold of the fear of God are emboldened by the help of God, and having lost this, they find a strength even stronger; and most magnificent are those who defend themselves in the name of Christ and of the Lord alone against enemies both visible and invisible (Ps 117:10-11).

He sings of the Lord's clear manifestation, through which salvation is restored to all, having said 'God' according to the Father and 'Lord' according to the Son's name, because both the Lord is God and the God is Lord; having appeared as Lord, He ruled over us and them into life, according to the [text breaks] that He might rule over the dead and the living, and the opposites into judgment (Ps 117:27a).
According to the abolishing of all authority and power (Ps 117:27bc).

The establishment of a feast is protected by a multitude of priests placing [sacrifices] upon the altar even unto its horns and the other projections. And as proceeding upon our own priests, the Word clearly shows those presenting themselves as a living sacrifice, truly pleasing to God according to a type of Christ (Ps 118:1), whose multitude also fills the altar even to the uppermost height which joins with the heavenly angels, through the same power which lifts the heavenly things toward the height and lifts up the earthly things by the manner of an altar receiving those approaching God.

These indeed were those not having walked in the counsel of the ungodly nor standing in the way of sinners (Ps 118:1bc), but grasping the law and the course in this. And he says 'blameless,' not meaning altogether falling away from faults and sins. For this was appointed for Christ and for the partakers of Christ through him; but for those, the blamelessness was judged by the forgiveness from God and not by the exactness regarding the outward regulations. For God does not require the impossible, but legislates by exposing what is lacking, and he forgives the weak, knowing them, and providing salvation through the then-yet-to-come participation in Christ, the powerful God. It is therefore fitting for us to live blamelessly according to Christ.

Since there were many oppositions toward virtue (Ps 118:5), just as there are stumbles on a road, he asks for the removal of these. For thus the road is made smooth by the removal of those who obstruct, according to 'Cast out of the way of my people the worms'; just as for the divine David a woman became a stumbling block and an unseasonable fall in a spectacle, for another a morsel for pleasure being seen, such as for Esau, for another glory just as for Saul, for another property just as for Ahab; all of which are necessary for God who is preparing the way, which should pack these things and maintain the beautiful inclination, even though the more violent things of the intention were pulling and, as if unwearying, were flowing because of their nature.

But for us, regarding the divine Spirit, it will be a matter of not being ashamed (Ps 118:6), when we see ourselves joined to him everywhere and in no way turning toward the flesh, nor being dragged down from a height of falling. In having learned the judgments of the...
In having learned the judgments of the...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Utility of Divine Wisdom and the Vanity of Mind
english: I will keep your statutes of righteousness. He says it asks for understanding, and it is promised that this will not be unfruitful. For I will not only learn, he says, but I will also keep your statutes (Ps 118:10).

Akyllas says, 'Let me not be ignorant' [toward what we are saying]. One using desire regarding the law fears the lack of understanding, which turns the zeal of many into the opposite. And in those things in which they seem to be upright, they have stumbled according to that which is said by Solomon: 'There is a way that seems right to men, but its end comes into the pit of Sheol' (Prov 14:12). For understanding does not come immediately from memory, but from the divine illumination; and the statutes are those capable of justifying (Ps 118:12b).

Pride is the mother of lawlessness. For through this they do not endure to obey the commands of God, such as the disobedient people who say, 'We will not be ruled, nor will we come to you anymore.' This shows his own readiness toward obeying the commandments to God. For he understands the guilty, and he will rebuke those who are disobedient and unruly through pride.

He prays to flee from the ignominy which is before God, which the Lord shows to be most fearful, saying that those who have shamed Him will be shamed (Ps 118:22). The lawful man, pointing out the opposite of this, says here mocking, [that they] are not to depart from the study of the holy oracles and the correction through them, and shortly after, he says, 'I have spoken in your testimonies against kings, and I was not ashamed' (Ps 118:23); such is also Paul, saying, 'For I am not ashamed of the gospel' (Rom 1:16).

What he himself says is to be a sacrifice to God, a broken and humbled heart, he says has now been fulfilled, having brought the soul down as to the ground and having been humbled voluntarily, just as regarding involuntary humbling it is said, 'Our soul was humbled into dust, our womb clung to the earth' (Ps 29:9). Having brought himself as becomes a humble man, he seeks from God a reward: a life-conduct according to the law and life according to the word of God (Ps 118:25). And this very thing is humbling: not to set the good life upon oneself, but to seek it from God.
To do all things greatly as in the eyes of God and to say these things and to recount (Ps 118:26-27).

And to ask for a corrective or confirming revelation regarding these things, while there remains for him also the benefit to others by conversing with a more divine understanding and announcing the wonderful benefit which God has stored up for those doing what is holy. For he who teaches concerning righteousness also teaches concerning the end, which is laid up for it, being something wonderful and unexpected, that God greatly and beyond measure rewards. Paul also conversed concerning self-control and righteousness and the judgment that is to come, as the ruler becomes a terror. Instead of 'I will not wander,' one [says] 'Akylas will preach,' and the other 'Symmachus will explain.'

If the heart of man is carefully directed toward evil from youth, it is necessary that God, by moving it toward righteous commands—that is, by leading our choice toward economies and realities and the illumination of the Holy Spirit—[intervene].

Vanity is the madness concerning visions, the contemplation concerning non-existent things, and the absurd fantasy according to the intellect, which Paul makes clear, saying, 'Being darkened in the vanity of their mind, having been alienated from the life of God' (Rom 1:21). See that 'vanity of mind' is called so when one has a mind and does not use it for the contemplation of the truths, but provides it to the binding Satan. This, therefore, he says, 'Turn my eyes away, lest I see vanity'; for this is by the grace of God. For in this way one will be able, having turned away from such an understanding, to live in the way of God, walking in it and making oneself alive by it; for at once to be the way is to be life. Therefore the Savior says, 'I am the way and the life' (John 14:6).
And since the Son is the righteousness of the Father, he says this regarding one desiring to live in the Son; for the righteousness of God is revealed in him from faith to faith (Rom 1:17).

He says only that it is sufficient for us to be comforted in afflictions to have the promise of true life; 'fulfill this for us.' For if in this life only we are hoping in Christ, we are more to be pitied than all men, because we suffer evil now and not in expectation of a life to come. But the life that is to come is a resuscitation, since the soul itself is not life, nor is it true life.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Stability of Righteousness and Divine Life
english: We learn, if indeed the soul is not a human. For if it had the truth of living in its own life, the dead would not need resuscitation. Therefore the Lord said to the dead to live as if they did not yet have life, except insofar as they are in the power of the life-giving God; and he says they are lost if they do not happen to have a resurrection, saying he will raise his own, so that the one from it might not be lost. And Paul similarly says, 'If there is no resurrection of the dead, then those who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished' (1 Cor 15:17). For God did not give a life to the soul from the beginning as incorporeal, but immediately the one in the body, having breathed the breath of life into the body.

Regarding Psalm 118:53, to the sinner, godliness is a laughing matter, but to the God-fearing, lawlessness is a terror, because he foresees the dread of punishment. Regarding Psalm 118:54, he says, 'To me, also, the judgments looking toward your commandments are my only consolation, and your precepts, being taken up through song, bring cheer and lead to joy' (Ps 118:54). And I have known this alone as one who will dwell in a foreign and strange land and is truly unable to have any good, because for a stranger, houses are longed for, and before the return to these things, all is sorrowful.

Regarding Psalm 118:73, God does not twist the justice of man like a potter, even if it is said he twists; rather, whatever a potter works, he makes such by the power of the one working such a shape; and the present-day 'moldings' must be referred back to that first molding, such as 'Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you' (Jer 1:5); just as Job says, 'You formed me from clay' (Job 10:9), indicating the clay-molding in Adam regarding himself. Prayer regarding the making is thanksgiving, but following this is the power of the intellect which understands the commandments. Concerning this, Paul also says, 'Understand what I say: for the Lord will give you understanding in all things' (Rom 11:33). But treat the request as if toward a Creator: 'Care for your handiwork, and complete with intellect the living thing that is intellectual; and that which you prepared for indwelling with yourself, make it indwell through your knowledge of Your purposes.' Since from the beginning, man was in need of that which, of the many commands, made his mind unsuited to them, and indeed, having been made unstable, he needs those which fulfill the greater.

For without training in many evils and without the hope of God's helping, a man cannot stand firmly in virtue, for those competing are easily shaken when the struggle comes. Thus, he recognizes the strengthening from many sufferings, the strengthening of God's providence; then he asks for rest from his labors, saying, 'Let your mercy come that it may comfort me according to your word' (Ps 118:83).

Perhaps the righteous become more dead than living under afflictions, as if they resemble ascetics rather than men, losing their souls like dust being blown about, while choosing the hot and the practical way, as it is said elsewhere, 'I sat in darkness as if dead to the age' (Ps 118:84); but even while undergoing this, he says, I have not departed from God-taught righteousness, just as Joseph guarded righteous temperance. He calls the commandments 'promises.' He says, 'With courage, I seek the help from you, my God, through your promises and their truth' (Ps 118:86).

He asks for life, not yet eternal life, but the present life, worthy of not being handed over to the hands of the schemers unto death (Ps 118:88). He does not ask for this as an end, but as a means to a good end, for he says, 'I will guard the commands of God,' through which it is also possible to acquire eternal life. 'I will cling to your laws,' he says (Ps 118:93). For in them is life found, just as you have said to me, 'He who has made them, man, shall live in them.'

Thus the righteous lives alone even if he seems to have died, but the unrighteous are dead even if they seem to live. For the former have the constitution of life within them, which is righteousness, but those not having this resemble soulless things moved not by themselves but from without, because their life is from without, and they do not even have one life within them. Therefore the Lord himself, being truly righteousness, declares himself to be life, and says those not partaking of him do not have life within themselves; and the death of the Savior is not only life but is life-giving, becoming the release of men from death. The unrighteous, moreover, are blind to the beauty of righteousness and the majesty of the words concerning it.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
